package_info.package_versions: All published versions (as flagged in report)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are considered malicious because they are published to public registries with names that match internal or private dependencies used by organizations, exploiting the dependency confusion attack vector. This can result in unintentional installation and execution of attacker-controlled code in victim environments, potentially leading to data exfiltration or system compromise. Many of these packages are proof-of-concept (PoC) demonstrations, but the attack technique is inherently dangerous and can be weaponized.

execution_context.trigger: import-time or install-time (depending on package type and configuration)
execution_context.file_location: package entry point (e.g., index.js for npm, __init__.py or setup.py for PyPI)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or install-time, the code logs a message to the console or standard output, demonstrating that arbitrary code can be executed if the package is installed due to dependency confusion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code executes automatically upon installation or import, which is highly suspicious, especially in packages with names matching internal dependencies. This demonstrates the ability to execute arbitrary code in victim environments, a key risk in supply chain attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not execute arbitrary code on install or import without explicit user action. These packages are designed to prove that code execution is possible via dependency confusion, violating the expectation of safe, inert package installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages may log messages or perform setup actions at install/import, but not for the purpose of demonstrating or exploiting dependency confusion. Legitimate use cases are rare and typically well-documented.
key_indicators: Package name matches known internal or private dependencies
Code in entry point files (index.js, __init__.py, setup.py) executes automatically on install/import
No legitimate functionality beyond PoC demonstration
May access environment variables or perform network operations (in more advanced PoCs)

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes a package to a public registry (npm or PyPI) with a name matching an internal or private dependency used by a target organization.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim's build or CI/CD system installs the malicious package from the public registry instead of the intended internal one.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in the package executes at install-time or import-time, logging a message or potentially exfiltrating data to demonstrate code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Proof-of-concept demonstration of code execution or, in a real attack, compromise of the build environment.

behavioral_signatures: Appearance of package names matching internal or private dependencies on public registries
Automatic code execution in entry point files (index.js, __init__.py, setup.py) during install/import
Unexpected logging or access to environment variables at install/import time
file_indicators: index.js, __init__.py, or setup.py containing code that executes on import or install
Packages with minimal or no legitimate functionality, often limited to logging or environment variable access
network_indicators: Outbound network requests initiated during install/import (if exfiltration is attempted)
Connections to domains or IPs controlled by the attacker (if present in code)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for installation of packages from public registries whose names match internal or private dependencies. Flag packages that execute code on install/import, especially if they perform network operations or access sensitive environment variables. Use allow-lists for approved package sources and names, and block or quarantine suspicious packages pending review. Implement automated scanning of entry point files for unexpected code execution patterns.
